n: MICAS - Malta International Contemporary Art Space
w: Built into the San Salvatore bastions above the Grand Harbour, this 4,000-square-metre venue opened in 2024 as Malta's first dedicated space for international contemporary art. Vaulted 17th-century magazines and old ammunition stores now hold large-scale installations, video and sculpture behind fortress walls.
s: Contemporary art built into a 17th-century fortress
why: Malta's first major contemporary art museum, opened 2024 inside historic bastions

w: An 18th-century palazzo beside the Pinacoteca di Brera, half a century in planning, finally opened in December 2024 to house Milan's 20th-century collection: Boccioni, Morandi and Modigliani alongside the Jesi and Vitali bequests of Futurist and modern works, plus rotating contemporary exhibitions.
s: Milan's long-delayed modern art palazzo, opened 2024
why: A 50-years-in-planning museum completing Milan's Brera art quarter

w: A disused 1930s electrical substation below Petrin Hill was rebuilt as a private, non-collecting kunsthalle, opening in February 2022 with eight exhibitions a year of Czech and international modern and contemporary art. Its industrial concrete transformer halls now host kinetic art, sculpture and video installations.
s: Contemporary art inside an old power substation
why: Prague's first major private kunsthalle, opened 2022

w: Fifty-one slender cast-iron figures, each abstracted from a laser scan of a Menzies resident, stand scattered across ten square kilometres of a dry outback salt lake. Installed for the 2003 Perth Festival and never removed, it has become one of the largest permanent outdoor sculpture installations on earth.
s: 51 iron figures scattered across a dry salt lake
why: Antony Gormley's largest permanent outdoor work, in remote outback WA

w: A private working farm on the Kaipara Harbour doubles as a sculpture park holding outdoor pieces by Richard Serra, Anish Kapoor, Andy Goldsworthy and Neil Dawson, scattered across rolling paddocks grazed by exotic livestock. Entry is free, but the farm opens to the public only a handful of days each year.
s: Monumental sculpture on a working farm by the harbour
why: One of the world's largest private outdoor sculpture collections

w: Fifty years and roughly 40 million dollars in the making, Michael Heizer's mile-and-a-half-long earthwork of sculpted concrete mounds, ramps and mesas rises from a remote high-desert valley. Completed in 2022, it admits only six visitors a day by reservation, making it one of the hardest artworks on earth to see.
s: A mile-long earthwork, 50 years in the making
why: The largest contemporary sculpture ever built, finished after half a century

w: Belgian sculptor Albert Szukalski's ghostly plaster-shrouded Last Supper figures stand in open desert beside the abandoned mining town of Rhyolite, joined since 1984 by a pink cinderblock couch, a mosaic sofa girl and other outdoor sculptures. Free and unstaffed, it sits at the edge of Death Valley.
s: Ghost-town sculpture garden on the Death Valley edge
why: Free, always-open outdoor sculpture museum beside a genuine ghost town

n: MACAAL - Museum of African Contemporary Art Al Maaden
w: Set among gardens and olive groves on the edge of Marrakech, this private museum opened in 2016 to show and champion contemporary African and diaspora art from the Lazraq family's collection. Rotating exhibitions of painting, sculpture and photography give African artists a platform outside Europe's museum framework.
s: Contemporary African art in a Marrakech garden museum
why: A leading platform for African contemporary art, built from a private collection

w: Forested trails on the ridge that once inspired Edvard Munch's The Scream now carry roughly 40 sculptures by Rodin, Renoir, Dali, Louise Bourgeois and Damien Hirst above the Oslofjord. Opened in 2013 on the 80th anniversary of Norway's occupation, the park is free to enter and never closes.
s: Forty sculptures on a ridge above the Oslofjord
why: A free, always-open sculpture trail with sweeping views over Oslo

w: Spanish sculptor Cristina Iglesias built a bronze-and-glass dome pierced with star-shaped openings for the royal parkland of Djurgarden, the founding work of a new permanent sculpture park backed by the Princess Estelle Cultural Foundation. Light and shadow shift through its perforations across the day.
s: A perforated bronze dome in a royal Stockholm park
why: Anchor piece of a new permanent sculpture park on royal land

w: Ninety hectares of parkland in China's industrial northeast hold more than 340 sculptures by artists from over 130 countries, gathered through international symposia since the park opened in 2003. Surrealist bronzes and stone monoliths sit half-hidden among trees, forming a vast open-air collection.
s: 340-plus sculptures from 130 countries in one park
why: One of the world's largest international outdoor sculpture collections

n: The Sculpture Park at Madhavendra Palace
w: India's first contemporary sculpture park fills the courtyards and chambers of an 18th-century hilltop palace above Jaipur, pairing site-specific works by Indian and international artists against frescoed walls and desert views. A yearly rotating exhibition keeps the dialogue between old fort and new art moving.
s: Contemporary sculpture inside a hilltop 18th-century fort
why: India's first contemporary sculpture park, staged inside a historic palace

w: A textile-district gallery east of the Imperial Palace opened in 2022 with a program shaped by anime aesthetics, digital culture and the friction between virtual and physical worlds. Since then it has grown from a neighbourhood fixture into one of Tokyo's most closely watched young artist-run spaces.
s: Digital-culture art gallery in Tokyo's old textile district
why: A fast-rising artist-run space shaping Tokyo's younger art scene

w: A former home on Charoen Krung, Thailand's first modern road, has been converted into a contemporary art space embedded in one of Bangkok's oldest riverside neighbourhoods. Exhibitions by Thai and international artists unfold inside a building whose own history of trade and migration mirrors the district outside.
s: Contemporary gallery in a historic riverside Bangkok house
why: Rising artist-run space in Bangkok's oldest trading quarter

w: More than 170 building facades across Lodz carry large-scale murals, the legacy of a project the Urban Forms Foundation began in 2009 that turned a fading textile city into Poland's biggest open-air gallery. Piotrkowska Street alone holds giant portraits, a Witcher mural and Poland's largest single mural.
s: 170-plus murals across a former textile city
why: Poland's largest concentration of large-scale street murals

w: Architect Thomas Phifer's luminous white concrete building opened in October 2024 opposite the Palace of Culture, giving Warsaw's modern art collection a permanent home after two decades in temporary venues. Galleries hold Polish neo-avant-garde and contemporary work beneath a rooftop terrace over the city centre.
s: Warsaw's new white concrete modern art museum, 2024
why: A landmark new building finally housing Poland's modern art collection

w: Founded in 2024, this artist-led gallery expanded across three sites within a single year: a Trafalgar street storefront, an experimental offshoot in Sarria and a private research residency on Menorca. Shows mix emerging Catalan artists with international names, run at the improvisational pace of an artist collective.
s: Fast-growing artist-run gallery, founded 2024
why: One of Barcelona's fastest-expanding new artist-run spaces

w: Founded in 2007, this Victoria Island foundation built LagosPhoto, West Africa's first major photography festival, alongside residencies and a National Art Competition that has launched careers across painting, video, ceramics and performance. Its gallery gives Lagos a year-round venue for contemporary African art.
s: Lagos gallery behind West Africa's top photo festival
why: Nigeria's leading platform for contemporary African photography and art

w: Curator Koyo Kouoh founded this Dakar centre in 2008 as an independent space for art, knowledge and society, running exhibitions, a library and an artist residency that made it one of West Africa's most institutionally consequential contemporary art venues. It anchors Dakar's gallery scene during the Dak'Art biennial.
s: Independent Dakar art centre and residency, since 2008
why: West Africa's most influential independent contemporary art institution

w: Once one of the most violent neighbourhoods in Latin America, this hillside barrio reinvented itself through murals by local artists like Chota13, using outdoor escalators built in 2011 to carry visitors up a slope now covered in colour. The paintings memorialise conflict while declaring transformation.
s: Murals covering outdoor escalators up a hillside barrio
why: A neighbourhood's rebirth told through community mural art

w: Artist Tia-Thuy Nguyen converted a cluster of shipping containers in the Thao Dien district into Saigon's first space dedicated purely to contemporary art when it opened in 2016. Rotating exhibitions, talks and a resident cafe made it a hub for Vietnamese artists in a market long ruled by tourist-trade painting.
s: Vietnam's first dedicated contemporary art centre
why: Ho Chi Minh City's leading purpose-built contemporary art venue

w: Artists founded this riverside park in 1986 to replant gardens flooded by a 1982 disaster, filling it since with roughly 40 sculptures by Chilean and international artists, from Marta Colvin's founding bronze Pachamama to rotating contemporary pieces. Entry is free along the Mapocho River in Providencia.
s: Forty sculptures reborn from a flood-ravaged riverbank
why: Chile's leading free open-air contemporary sculpture collection

n: Parque del Amor and El Beso
w: Victor Delfin's mosaic-covered sculpture of two entwined lovers, unveiled on Valentine's Day 1993, anchors a clifftop park along Lima's Costa Verde. Wavy Gaudi-style benches ring the statue while paragliders launch from the cliffs behind it, above the Pacific surf of Miraflores.
s: A giant lovers' sculpture on a Lima clifftop park
why: Lima's best-loved public sculpture, on a dramatic ocean bluff

w: Opened in 2024 as the only private art foundation on Saadiyat Island's Cultural District, this non-profit gives public access to a private collection through a main gallery, an annex and a sculpture garden, running alongside the district's Louvre Abu Dhabi and future Guggenheim outposts.
s: Private art foundation newly opened on Saadiyat Island
why: The only private art foundation inside Abu Dhabi's museum district

w: A 100-metre steel cube clad in nearly 10,000 square metres of mirror sits in a desert canyon near AlUla, reflecting the sandstone cliffs and sky until its walls seem to dissolve into the landscape. Opened in 2019 and holding a Guinness record as the largest mirrored building on earth, it also serves as a concert hall.
s: The world's largest mirrored building, in a desert canyon
why: A record-holding mirrored landmark anchoring Saudi Arabia's new art valley

w: Alexandre Farto, known as Vhils, chisels and drills portraits directly into building walls rather than painting them, and this carved face of an elderly woman on a Cais do Sodre facade is among his best-known works. His subtractive technique treats the crumbling plaster of the wall itself as the medium.
s: A portrait carved, not painted, into a Lisbon wall
why: Signature work by Portugal's best-known street artist, using chisel not spray can

w: Founded in 2013 and moved into a larger Lavington space in 2023, this gallery built East Africa's most consistent platform for contemporary art, running roughly eight exhibitions a year plus an annual modern and East African art auction that has become a benchmark for the region's market.
s: East Africa's leading contemporary art gallery and auction
why: The region's benchmark gallery for East African contemporary art
